assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Fix integers m >= 2 and g >= 0. Encode numerical semigroups of multiplicity m by Kunz-coordinate tuples using the Apéry set. The Kunz inequalities characterize exactly which tuples arise, and the genus equals the sum of the coordinates. Therefore N(m,g) is the cardinality of the finite set K_{m,g} of Kunz vectors with coordinate sum g. Next, for each x in K_{m,g}, choose the least coordinate whose increment preserves the Kunz inequalities; existence of such a coordinate gives a well-defined map Phi from K_{m,g} to K_{m,g+1}. A separate reconstruction lemma shows that the least coadmissible coordinate of Phi(x) recovers the incremented coordinate, so Phi is injective. By the basic fact that an injection between finite sets implies a cardinality inequality, |K_{m,g}| <= |K_{m,g+1}|. Translating back through the Kunz correspondence gives N(m,g) <= N(m,g+1), which is exactly the theorem.

steps.derives: For every integer m >= 2 and every integer g >= 0, if K_{m,g} denotes the set of tuples x = (x_1,...,x_{m-1}) of positive integers satisfying the Kunz inequalities for multiplicity m and having coordinate sum g, then N(m,g) = |K_{m,g}|.
steps.trivial_justification: L1 gives the Apéry/Kunz encoding of numerical semigroups of multiplicity m by positive integer tuples. L2 identifies exactly which tuples encode numerical semigroups: namely those satisfying the Kunz inequalities. L3 states that the genus of the semigroup encoded by x is exactly x_1 + ... + x_{m-1}. Therefore the numerical semigroups counted by N(m,g) are in bijection with the tuples in K_{m,g}, so N(m,g) = |K_{m,g}|.

steps.derives: For every integers m >= 2 and g >= 0, the rule Phi(x) = x + e_{alpha(x)}, where alpha(x) is the least admissible index of x, defines a function Phi : K_{m,g} -> K_{m,g+1}.
steps.trivial_justification: By L4, every x in K_{m,g} has at least one admissible index, so alpha(x) is well-defined. By L5, the corresponding tuple Phi(x) belongs to K_{m,g+1}. Hence Phi is a well-defined function from K_{m,g} to K_{m,g+1}.

steps.derives: For every integers m >= 2 and g >= 0, the function Phi : K_{m,g} -> K_{m,g+1} is injective.
steps.trivial_justification: L6 proves a stronger statement on the full Kunz set K_m: for any x in K_m, the least coadmissible index of Phi(x) recovers the least admissible index of x, and therefore Phi(x) = Phi(x') implies x = x'. Since K_{m,g} is a subset of K_m and Phi maps K_{m,g} into K_{m,g+1}, the restriction of Phi to K_{m,g} is injective.

steps.derives: For every integers m >= 2 and g >= 0, |K_{m,g}| <= |K_{m,g+1}|.
steps.trivial_justification: Apply the finite-set injection principle to the injective map Phi : K_{m,g} -> K_{m,g+1} obtained in A3.

steps.derives: For every integer m >= 2 and every integer g >= 0, the number N(m,g) of numerical semigroups having multiplicity m and genus g satisfies N(m,g) <= N(m,g+1).
steps.trivial_justification: By A1, N(m,g) = |K_{m,g}| and N(m,g+1) = |K_{m,g+1}|. By A4, |K_{m,g}| <= |K_{m,g+1}|. Substituting these equalities into the inequality yields exactly N(m,g) <= N(m,g+1).

lemmas.role_in_assembly: Introduces the Kunz-coordinate model for numerical semigroups of fixed multiplicity.
lemmas.statement_nl: Let m be an integer with m >= 2. Let S be a numerical semigroup whose multiplicity is m. For each residue i with 1 <= i <= m-1, let w_i be the least element of S congruent to i modulo m, and write w_i = m x_i + i. Then each x_i is a positive integer, and the tuple x = (x_1,...,x_{m-1}) determines S uniquely by the rule S = {0} union {q m + w_i : 1 <= i <= m-1, q in N0} union {q m : q in N0}. Conversely, every choice of positive integers x_1,...,x_{m-1} determines a unique set of this form once the closure conditions for a numerical semigroup are satisfied.

lemmas.role_in_assembly: Characterizes which integer tuples correspond to numerical semigroups of multiplicity m.
lemmas.statement_nl: Let m be an integer with m >= 2, and let x = (x_1,...,x_{m-1}) be a tuple of positive integers. Define w_i = m x_i + i for 1 <= i <= m-1, and define S_x = {0} union {q m : q in N0} union {q m + w_i : q in N0 and 1 <= i <= m-1}. Then S_x is a numerical semigroup of multiplicity m if and only if the following Kunz inequalities hold for all i,j in {1,...,m-1}: if i + j < m, then x_i + x_j >= x_{i+j}; and if i + j > m, then x_i + x_j + 1 >= x_{i+j-m}.

lemmas.role_in_assembly: Converts the original counting problem into a problem about counting Kunz vectors with fixed coordinate sum.
lemmas.statement_nl: Let m be an integer with m >= 2, and let x = (x_1,...,x_{m-1}) be a tuple of positive integers satisfying the Kunz inequalities: for all i,j in {1,...,m-1}, if i + j < m then x_i + x_j >= x_{i+j}, and if i + j > m then x_i + x_j + 1 >= x_{i+j-m}. Let S_x = {0} union {q m : q in N0} union {q m + (m x_i + i) : q in N0 and 1 <= i <= m-1}. Then the genus of S_x equals x_1 + x_2 + ... + x_{m-1}. Consequently, for every integer g >= 0, the number N(m,g) of numerical semigroups of multiplicity m and genus g equals the number of tuples x in (Z_{>0})^(m-1) satisfying the Kunz inequalities and x_1 + ... + x_{m-1} = g.

lemmas.role_in_assembly: Provides existence of a one-step genus-raising move on every Kunz vector.
lemmas.statement_nl: Let m be an integer with m >= 2, and let x = (x_1,...,x_{m-1}) be a tuple of positive integers satisfying the Kunz inequalities: for all i,j in {1,...,m-1}, if i + j < m then x_i + x_j >= x_{i+j}, and if i + j > m then x_i + x_j + 1 >= x_{i+j-m}. Call an index r in {1,...,m-1} admissible for x if the tuple x + e_r, obtained by replacing x_r with x_r + 1 and leaving all other coordinates unchanged, also satisfies the same Kunz inequalities. Then at least one admissible index exists for every such tuple x.

lemmas.role_in_assembly: Defines the canonical map between the level-g and level-(g+1) Kunz sets and proves it lands in the correct target set.
lemmas.statement_nl: Let m be an integer with m >= 2, and let K_{m,g} be the set of all tuples x = (x_1,...,x_{m-1}) of positive integers such that x satisfies the Kunz inequalities for multiplicity m, namely: for all i,j in {1,...,m-1}, if i + j < m then x_i + x_j >= x_{i+j}, and if i + j > m then x_i + x_j + 1 >= x_{i+j-m}, and such that x_1 + ... + x_{m-1} = g. For x in K_{m,g}, define alpha(x) to be the smallest index r in {1,...,m-1} for which x + e_r also satisfies the Kunz inequalities, and define Phi(x) = x + e_{alpha(x)}. Then Phi(x) belongs to K_{m,g+1} for every x in K_{m,g}.

lemmas.role_in_assembly: Establishes injectivity of the canonical genus-raising map on Kunz vectors.
lemmas.statement_nl: Let m be an integer with m >= 2, and let K_m be the set of all tuples y = (y_1,...,y_{m-1}) of positive integers satisfying the Kunz inequalities for multiplicity m: for all i,j in {1,...,m-1}, if i + j < m then y_i + y_j >= y_{i+j}, and if i + j > m then y_i + y_j + 1 >= y_{i+j-m}. For y in K_m, call an index s in {1,...,m-1} coadmissible for y if y_s > 1 and the tuple y - e_s also belongs to K_m. Let beta(y) be the smallest coadmissible index of y whenever such an index exists. For x in K_m, call an index r admissible for x if x + e_r belongs to K_m, let alpha(x) be the smallest admissible index, and define Phi(x) = x + e_{alpha(x)}. Then for every x in K_m, the tuple Phi(x) has at least one coadmissible index and in fact beta(Phi(x)) = alpha(x). Consequently, if x and x' are elements of K_m and Phi(x) = Phi(x'), then x = x'.

lemmas.role_in_assembly: Converts the injective map on Kunz-vector sets into the desired inequality of counts.

For m=3, x=(2,2) and x'=(3,1) are both valid Kunz vectors, but the least-admissible-index map gives Phi(x)=Phi(x')=(3,2), so A3 fails and the rest of the counting argument collapses. assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Fix integers m >= 2 and g >= 0, and let SG(m,g) be the family of numerical semigroups with multiplicity m and genus g. First, use the Apéry-coordinate genus formula to know that SG(m,g) is finite, and similarly SG(m,g+1) is finite. Next define a canonical child map on SG(m,g) by deleting the element F(S)+m, where F(S) is the Frobenius number of S. The key semigroup-theoretic facts are that F(S)+m belongs to S, is a minimal generator of S, and deleting it produces a numerical semigroup of the same multiplicity and one larger genus; moreover the Frobenius number of the child is exactly the deleted element. Hence Psi(S)=S\{F(S)+m} is a well-defined map SG(m,g)->SG(m,g+1). The identity F(Psi(S))=F(S)+m shows that the removed element can be recovered from the child, so S = Psi(S) ∪ {F(Psi(S))}; therefore Psi is injective. Since both source and target families are finite, the injection implies |SG(m,g)| <= |SG(m,g+1)|. Finally, by definition N(m,g)=|SG(m,g)| and N(m,g+1)=|SG(m,g+1)|, yielding N(m,g) <= N(m,g+1).

steps.trivial_justification: L5 states exactly that for every S in SG(m,g), the set Psi(S) is a numerical semigroup of multiplicity m and genus g+1. Therefore the assignment S ↦ Psi(S) lands in SG(m,g+1) for every source element S, so it is a well-defined function from SG(m,g) to SG(m,g+1).

steps.derives: For fixed integers m >= 2 and g >= 0, the function Psi : SG(m,g) -> SG(m,g+1) is injective.
steps.trivial_justification: L6 states that for every S in SG(m,g), one can reconstruct S from Psi(S) by the formula S = Psi(S) union {F(Psi(S))}. Hence if Psi(S) = Psi(S') for two elements S,S' of SG(m,g), then both reconstructions yield the same set, so S = S'. This is exactly injectivity of Psi.

steps.derives: For fixed integers m >= 2 and g >= 0, |SG(m,g)| <= |SG(m,g+1)|.
steps.trivial_justification: From A2, both SG(m,g) and SG(m,g+1) are finite. From A4, there exists an injective function Psi from SG(m,g) to SG(m,g+1). Applying L7 to these two finite sets and the injective map Psi yields the inequality |SG(m,g)| <= |SG(m,g+1)|.

steps.derives: For every integer m >= 2 and every integer g >= 0, the number N(m,g) of numerical semigroups with multiplicity m and genus g satisfies N(m,g) <= N(m,g+1).
steps.trivial_justification: By A1, N(m,g) equals |SG(m,g)| and N(m,g+1) equals |SG(m,g+1)|. By A5, |SG(m,g)| <= |SG(m,g+1)|. Substituting the equalities from A1 into the inequality from A5 gives exactly N(m,g) <= N(m,g+1).

Then x is a minimal generator of S: x belongs to S, x is positive, and whenever a and b are positive elements of S with x = a + b, one must have a = 0 or b = 0.
